result.question: Code-organization norms for Python and TypeScript projects (2024-2026): (1) file/module and function SIZE norms — what style guides and lint tools actually prescribe or default to (ESLint max-lines / max-lines-per-function, Pylint module/function limits, ruff C901/PLR complexity, SonarQube/CodeClimate thresholds, Google/Airbnb guidance), any empirical link between size and defect rates/maintainability, and practitioner guidance on enforcing size caps on LLM/agent-generated code; (2) FOLDER STRUCTURE — folder-by-feature vs folder-by-type and the colocation principle, with framework guidance (Angular, React, FastAPI, Django); (3) BARREL FILES (index.ts re-exports) — the tree-shaking / bundle-size / circular-dependency / test-performance case against them and when they're still acceptable; (4) llms.txt — adoption state in 2026 and whether coding agents actually consume it, i.e. is it worth generating for a code repo; (5) new-project setup defaults — pnpm workspaces / turborepo and monorepo-vs-single-package for TypeScript 2025-2026, plus pytest layout/naming/fixtures and pre-commit conventions for Python.

Angles are anchored to 2024-2026 and to named tools/frameworks so results surface primary style-guide and lint-config sources rather than generic blog opinion.

results.title: Barrel Files: Why index.ts Re-Exports Hurt Tree Shaking, Next.js Dev Memory, and tsc (2026)
results.snippet: Most complete treatment of the anti-pattern with hard numbers. Ties barrel files to the three canonical failure modes — bundles that don't tree-shake, Next.js dev/tsc getting slower and memory-hungry as the app grows, and circular-dep 'Cannot access X before initialization' bugs. Cites a real case: a dev page importing a single hook pulled a 552 kB client chunk that dropped to 64 kB once the barrel was removed. Prescriptive: import straight from the source file inside app code; barrels remain fine for pure type-definition libraries since types have zero bundle impact.

results.title: Tree shaking doesn't work with TypeScript barrel files (vercel/next.js issue #12557)
results.snippet: Canonical upstream evidence that the tree-shaking problem is real and tool-level, not folklore. Long-running Next.js/webpack issue documenting that re-export barrels defeat dead-code elimination, pulling unused sibling modules into the bundle. Primary-source grounding for the 'stop using barrel files' rationale and context for Next.js's later optimizePackageImports workaround.

results.title: Why I Prefer Barrel Files in 2026 — Codecompose
results.snippet: The deliberate counterpoint / 'when still acceptable' case, which the original question explicitly asks for. Argues barrels remain worthwhile for public API surfaces and type-only re-exports where the tree-shaking/circular-dep costs don't apply, and where import ergonomics and refactor stability matter. Useful to avoid overstating the anti-pattern as absolute.

results.title: The Hidden Costs of Barrel Files — wesionaryTEAM
results.snippet: Practitioner walkthrough of why barrels backfire: accidental over-importing (loading Button also loads Table, Chart, HeavyLibrary via a shared index.ts), slower cold-start and test runs, and circular-import fragility that appears in one tool but not another ('works in Vite, dies in Jest') because module evaluation order differs across bundler/Node/Jest.

results.title: Stop Killing Your Bundle Size (barrel files) — DEV Community
results.snippet: Representative of the mainstream 'stop using barrel files' trend the question probes. Frames barrels as a silent bundle-size regression and shows import-from-source as the fix. Good signal on current community consensus direction, lighter on empirical depth than the ReactUse piece.

results.title: Everything About Barrel Exports in JavaScript — 4markdown
results.snippet: Broad reference covering the mechanics of barrel exports, the pros (single import point, encapsulated module API) and the cons (tree-shaking defeat, circular dependencies, slower tooling), and guidance on scoping them narrowly. Useful as a balanced overview tying the trade-offs together rather than advocating one side.

results.title: The /llms.txt file, v2 – llms-txt (official spec)
results.snippet: The canonical spec (now at v2). Establishes what llms.txt actually is and the format coding tools parse. Load-bearing for judging whether it's worth generating for a code repo: the spec's own framing is that it's a curated, markdown-linked map of docs for LLM consumption, not an SEO artifact. Primary source, not commentary.

results.title: llms.txt Explained (May 2026): The Honest Guide to the Spec, Adoption, and How to Ship One
results.snippet: Most substantive of the guides: gives the '2026 honest read' that llms.txt is a developer-experience play, not an SEO play — worth it specifically when your readers are developers using AI-assisted IDEs. Names concrete adopters (Stripe, Vercel, Cloudflare, Anthropic, Cursor) shipping it because users build with coding agents. Directly answers sub-lane (4): worth generating for a code/dev-tool repo, near-zero cost (half-day manual, few hours CI).

Relevant for how context files (CLAUDE.md / llms.txt / rules files) fit a real 2026 coding workflow, rather than the marketing framing.

results.title: max-lines — ESLint (official rule docs)
results.snippet: Authoritative source for the exact ESLint default named in sub-lane (1): max-lines defaults to 300 lines per file. Config shape is ["error", { max: 300, skipBlankLines: false, skipComments: false }] — both skip options default false, so blank/comment lines count by default. This is the primary reference for a file-size cap on TS/JS (and LLM-generated code).

results.title: max-lines-per-function — ESLint (official rule docs)

results.title: too-many-lines / C0302 — Pylint documentation
results.snippet: Official Pylint reference for the module-size limit: too-many-lines (C0302) is governed by max-module-lines, which defaults to 1000 lines per module — the Python-side counterpart to ESLint's 300. Note the ~3x gap between the JS and Python defaults, useful when setting a cross-language house cap. (The all-options config page lists the same default.)

results.title: Default Analysis Configuration — Code Climate
results.snippet: Supplies Code Climate's concrete defaults for sub-lane (1): the file-lines check flags files over 250 lines by default (stricter than ESLint's 300), plus method-lines and complexity checks, and a hard 500KB cap above which a file is skipped entirely. Third independent tool default to triangulate a size threshold.

results.title: Google Python Style Guide
results.snippet: Named style guide from the question. Google's guides prescribe line-length (80 chars for Python) and structure/complexity guidance rather than a hard file-line cap — evidence that the major style guides constrain line width and function complexity but generally do NOT set numeric module-size limits, leaving that to lint tools. Google's shell guide separately advises rewriting scripts over ~100 lines in a structured language.

results.title: Airbnb JavaScript Style Guide
results.snippet: The other style guide named in the question. Airbnb's guide caps line length at 100 characters and pushes small, single-responsibility modules, but like Google sets no explicit max-file-lines number — reinforcing that file/module size ceilings come from lint defaults (ESLint 300, Pylint 1000, Code Climate 250), not from the prose style guides.

results.title: Colocation — Kent C. Dodds
results.snippet: The canonical statement of the colocation principle the question names directly: 'Place code as close to where it's relevant as possible' / 'things that change together should be located as close as reasonable.' Argues colocation reduces maintenance cost and improves applicability — the conceptual foundation for folder-by-feature over folder-by-type.

results.title: Organizing Code by Feature: How Colocation Makes Your Codebase Easier to Work With
results.snippet: Directly contrasts folder-by-type (layer: controllers/services/models) against folder-by-feature, showing that a single logical change in the layer pattern scatters edits across the tree. results.title: Layer pattern vs Module pattern — Folder Structure is Context Structure for AI

results.title: Screaming Architecture — Evolution of a React Folder Structure

results.title: Locality of Behavior / Co-location — Matias Kinnunen
results.snippet: Grounds colocation in the broader 'locality of behavior' principle (Carson Gross/HTMX), tying together why keeping related code physically adjacent aids readability and change-safety. Useful conceptual backing beyond framework-specific advice.

results.title: Production-Grade React Project Structure: From Setup to Scale
results.snippet: Prescriptive feature-based folder layout for scaling React/TypeScript apps, with the pragmatic hybrid (feature folders plus a shared layer) that most large projects converge on — matches the question's note that big projects mix both approaches.

results.title: Good Integration Practices — pytest documentation (official)
results.snippet: The authoritative source for sub-lane (5) Python side. Prescribes the src/ layout (src/mypkg/ + separate tests/ dir) so tests run against the installed package and catch packaging glitches; recommends importlib import mode for new projects (addopts=["--import-mode=importlib"] in pyproject.toml); explains conftest.py placement and that setuptools/pytest-runner integration is discouraged. This is the norm every blog below derives from.

results.title: Pytest Best Practices 2026: Fixtures, Markers, Config — QASkills.sh
results.snippet: Directly answers pytest convention norms (sub-lane 5): configure pytest in pyproject.toml with --strict-markers, use src layout with tests in a separate directory, centralize shared fixtures in conftest.py (never import them manually — pytest wires by name), and pick fixture scopes deliberately (function vs session) as the main determinant of suite speed. Concrete, current, convention-focused.

results.title: Python packaging: use the "src" layout — James Bennett
results.snippet: Well-regarded practitioner argument for the src/ layout (Bennett is a longtime Django contributor). Explains why a flat root layout lets pytest prepend the repo root to sys.path — masking packaging/import bugs — and why src/ forces you to test the installed package. Grounds the folder-structure + test-layout defaults in a reasoned 'why', not just a rule.

results.snippet: Core source for sub-lane (5) TS side and the single-vs-monorepo default question. Useful as the concrete setup companion to the higher-level best-practices piece.

Recommends direct internal imports over directory barrels.

claims.claim: Importing a single hook through the @reactuses/core barrel produced a 552 kB dev-mode client chunk; switching to per-module dist imports cut it to 64 kB (an ~88% reduction), because dev mode loaded all 120+ hooks despite only one being imported.
claims.quote: 552 kB dev-mode client chunk when importing a single hook (useDebounce) through @reactuses/core's barrel ... 64 kB after switching to per-module dist — an 88% reduction ... dev mode loaded 'all 120+ hooks, including the heavyweight ones' despite importing only one

claims.claim: Barrel files defeat tree-shaking when a module has top-level side effects (the bundler keeps everything), when output is CommonJS (shaking off entirely), or when transpiler artifacts like class fields/decorators/enums lack /*#__PURE__*/ annotations; and tree-shaking is a production-only optimization, so dev servers do not shake it out at all.
claims.quote: Side effects poison the whole barrel ... CommonJS output 'turns the shaking off entirely' ... tree shaking is a _production optimization_. Dev servers...do not shake.

claims.claim: TypeScript compile time and memory scale with the import graph rather than the code you use: a type-only reference to one hook through a barrel still parses all 120 modules, contributing to tsc slowdowns and language-server memory bloat.
claims.quote: `tsc` time and memory scale with the graph, not your code ... a type-only reference to one hook still parses 120 modules

claims.claim: A unit test importing one helper through a barrel evaluates the entire barrel, which is a classic cause of trivial test suites taking seconds per file to boot.
claims.quote: A unit test importing one helper through a barrel evaluates the whole barrel — a classic reason trivial test suites take seconds per file to boot.

claims.claim: Barrel files are not universally bad — a barrel grouping ~five cohesive files is fine, while a large app-wide barrel (e.g. components/index.ts with 300 exports) is the problem; for internal package imports the guidance is to import from the module, not the barrel.
claims.quote: A barrel that groups five cohesive files is fine ... App-wide `components/index.ts` with 300 exports is a bomb ... Import from the module, not the barrel

results.title: Theory of Relative Defect Proneness (Koru et al., Empirical Software Engineering)
results.snippet: Peer-reviewed empirical study establishing the counterintuitive 'relative defect proneness' finding: replicated across ten open-source products, the size-defect relationship follows a power law where defect proneness grows SLOWER than size, so smaller modules are proportionally MORE defect-prone per line than larger ones. Directly answers the unevidenced 'does size correlate with defects' gap — and cautions against a naive 'smaller is always safer' cap rationale.

results.title: Encapsulation and Optimal Module Size — Hatton's 'golden module size' (Raymond, TAOUP)
results.snippet: Synthesizes Hatton's empirical result that defect density vs. module size is a U-shaped curve: both very small and very large modules carry more bugs, with a minimum ('sweet spot') around 200-400 logical LOC (roughly 400-800 physical lines), language-independent. This is the canonical empirical basis for a size band rather than an arbitrary hard cap — the strongest single citation for the size→defect lane.

results.title: Thresholds for Size and Complexity Metrics: A Case Study from the Perspective of Defect Density
results.snippet: Case study deriving actual numeric thresholds for size/complexity metrics keyed to defect density — the empirical grounding for choosing a specific lint cap value rather than a folkloric one. Note it also reports there is no statistical evidence that files beyond some fixed size threshold are uniformly more defect-prone, tempering hard-cap claims.

results.title: Right-Sizing Your Python Files: The 150-500 Line Sweet Spot for AI Code Editors
results.snippet: Practitioner guidance aimed squarely at the LLM-code-cap gap: argues for keeping Python files in a 150-500 LOC band so an agent can hold the whole file in working context without truncation-driven errors. Frames the cap as a context-window / edit-reliability constraint specific to agent-generated code, not just human maintainability.

results.title: ESLint as AI Guardrails: 5 Rules That Make AI-Generated Code Readable
results.snippet: Concrete enforcement recipe for capping agent output: names specific ESLint rules including a ~50-line-per-function limit, with the key argument that linters are hard constraints an agent cannot ignore (unlike AGENTS.md/docs, which it can). Directly addresses 'enforcing size caps on LLM-generated code specifically' via CI-enforced max-lines / max-lines-per-function / complexity rules.

results.title: Maintainability Sensors for Coding Agents (martinfowler.com)
results.snippet: Authoritative practitioner treatment of automated 'sensors' (complexity, size, and maintainability signals) used to keep coding-agent output in check — the deterministic-guardrail framing for size/complexity caps on agent code. Higher-credibility counterpart to the blog posts, useful for the 'guardrails an agent cannot bypass' argument and for linking size limits to broader maintainability sensing.

result.summary: Across the five requested lanes the evidence is strong for size norms and folder structure, but thin-to-absent for barrel files, monorepo tooling, and pre-commit. On size: lint tools converge on low-hundreds line caps (ESLint defaults 300/file and 50/function-when-enabled; Pylint's C0302 too-many-lines message), yet ESLint's own rationale disclaims any objective maximum (100–500 is the "usual recommendation" band), the modern Code Climate successor Qlty gates on complexity (15/function, 50/file) rather than raw lines, and peer-reviewed empirical work actually finds smaller modules proportionally MORE defect-prone (power-law β<1) — the only AI-code-specific size caps (Python 150–500 LOC; 50/function + 250/file via ESLint) come from practitioner blogs, not consensus or data. On folder structure the consensus is clear and well-corroborated: the colocation principle (place code near where it is used) and folder-by-feature (the "module" pattern) are the recommended default for any new project expected to grow, over folder-by-type. pytest strongly recommends the src layout with test_*.py / *_test.py discovery naming. llms.txt is genuinely and widely PUBLISHED by 2026 (all three major AI labs plus auto-generating doc platforms), but the spec frames agent CONSUMPTION as intended-not-confirmed and field data is mixed, leaving its worthwhileness for a code repo unresolved. The barrel-files, pnpm/monorepo/turborepo, and pre-commit sub-lanes produced zero surviving claims and remain unevidenced.

findings.claim: Lint tools default to size caps in the low hundreds of lines and treat raw module length as a defect: ESLint's max-lines rule defaults to 300 lines/file, and max-lines-per-function defaults to 50 lines/function (the latter is OFF by default, so 50 applies only when the rule is explicitly enabled). ESLint's own rationale states there is no objective maximum acceptable file size but that common recommendations range 100–500 lines. Pylint ships a dedicated convention message, too-many-lines (C0302), that frames raw module length as a readability defect, governed by the configurable max-module-lines option (real default 1000; the docs' illustrative example sets it to 15).
findings.evidence: All five constituent claims verified verbatim against official primary docs and unanimously (3-0). ESLint: 'max (default 300)' for files, 'max (default 50)' for functions, plus the verbatim rationale 'not an objective maximum... Recommendations usually range from 100 to 500 lines.' Pylint C0302 'Too many lines in module (%s/%s)... reducing its readability' with '[main] max-module-lines = 15' as the doc example. Two precise qualifiers matter: max-lines-per-function is not in any recommended config (off by default), and Pylint's real default is 1000, not the doc's illustrative 15.

findings.claim: The modern Code Climate successor (Qlty) governs maintainability by a COMPLEXITY metric, not a raw line count: it defaults function-complexity to a cap of 15 and whole-file complexity to a cap of 50, and dropped Code Climate classic's raw line-count caps (file-lines 250, method-lines 25). LOC is still tracked as a maintainability metric/rating but is not part of the gating smell set.
findings.evidence: The cited Code Climate docs URL 301-redirects to docs.qlty.sh (its live successor). Qlty's config reference lists function_complexity = 15 ('Maximum function complexity') and file_complexity = 50 ('Maximum allowed complexity for a single file') as the all-languages default; its 8 code smells include 'High file complexity' and 'High function complexity' but NO raw line-count smell. Caveats (non-refuting): 15/50 is the base default with per-language overrides (Rust function_complexity 20), and Qlty still surfaces LOC as a Size Rating metric. Two related over-reaching claims about parameter-count defaults and the exact eight-check list were REFUTED 0-3.

findings.claim: Empirical evidence contradicts the intuition that larger files are riskier per unit size: peer-reviewed work (Koru et al., 2008, externally validated and independently replicated) finds defect proneness follows a power law D=α·s^β with β significantly below 1.0, so SMALLER modules are proportionally more defect-prone and defects accrue slower than size grows.
findings.evidence: Direction is well-supported by a primary peer-reviewed source across 10 KOffice products (all β<1.0), validated on 2 commercial systems (ACE, IBM-DB) and independently replicated (2010 closed-source study; companion IEEE Mozilla/JBoss/Eclipse study). Two load-bearing caveats keep this at medium not high: (1) 'proportionally' means per-unit — larger modules still have MORE total defects (β>0), so this is NOT evidence that large files are safe overall; (2) all data is human-authored C/C++/Java circa 2008–2014 and says nothing about LLM/agent-generated code. The specific β≈0.32–0.42 range in the claim is imprecise and doesn't match the cited paper's own values (~0.4–0.7). The opposing U-curve/sweet-spot model (Hatton via TAOUP) was separately REFUTED 0-3.

findings.claim: Practitioner guidance prescribes concrete size caps specifically for AI/agent-generated code: one article prescribes keeping Python files between 150 and 500 lines of actual code (blank lines and comments explicitly excluded); another prescribes ESLint 'AI guardrails' of max 50 lines/function (forces extraction) and max 250 lines/file (forces modularity), mapping to ESLint's max-lines-per-function and max-lines rules.
findings.evidence: Both are single practitioner Medium blogs; both were 403 bot-blocked on direct fetch, so corroboration is via two matching independent search-snippet passes plus ESLint's own docs confirming the rule mapping is real (max-lines-per-function default 50; max-lines with a custom 250). These are DESCRIPTIVE claims about what each article prescribes, so blog sourcing matches claim strength — but the specific numbers are individual opinion, not consensus or empirical fact. Notably, the article's stated RATIONALE (that 150–500 LOC is AI-working-memory-specific rather than classical maintainability) was REFUTED 0-3, so only the prescribed band survives, not its justification.

findings.claim: The colocation principle — popularized by Kent C. Dodds — is 'place code as close to where it's relevant as possible': keep related files (component, test, styles, data logic) physically close together in a feature folder, organized by what they belong to rather than by file type. It is the definitional basis of folder-by-feature.
findings.evidence: Core proposition verbatim from the canonical primary source (Dodds, who popularized the term): 'Place code as close to where it's relevant as possible' / 'things that change together should be located as close as reasonable.' Independently corroborated by React's own File Structure FAQ, seanmcp, koenvangilst. One nuance keeping honesty: colocation is technically BROADER than the feature-vs-type folder debate (it also covers colocating state, comments, CSS-in-JS, assets) — the 'i.e. organize by feature rather than by type' gloss is the mainstream corollary reading, not a literal equivalence in Dodds's article. Note the related claim that test files specifically should be co-located was REFUTED 0-3, so test placement is contested.

findings.claim: Current practitioner consensus (2024–2026) favors folder-by-feature (the 'module' pattern) over folder-by-type (the 'layer' pattern) for any new project expected to grow. Feature organization colocates all code for a domain so a new feature is added by adding one folder, whereas folder-by-type requires touching controllers/, services/, models/, and utils/ simultaneously to add a feature.

findings.claim: pytest strongly recommends the src layout (especially under its default 'prepend' import mode, though it recommends importlib mode for new projects), and its test-discovery convention collects files matching test_*.py or *_test.py, and within them functions/methods prefixed with 'test' (optionally inside Test-prefixed classes that have no __init__).
findings.evidence: Both claims verified verbatim against pytest's official goodpractices doc and confirmed identical on the GitHub main branch (not stale): 'especially if you use the default import mode prepend, it is strongly suggested to use a src layout' and the discovery rules 'test_*.py or *_test.py files' with 'test prefixed test functions or methods' inside/outside 'Test prefixed test classes.' Note pytest recommends importlib for NEW projects but prepend remains the DEFAULT, so the src-layout recommendation stands. A stronger claim that pytest recommends a SEPARATE top-level tests dir over colocation was REFUTED 0-3 — pytest documents both layouts, so test placement is not prescribed.

findings.evidence: Publishing facts are high-confidence (3-0): all three lab URLs verified live, and platform auto-generation independently corroborated (Yoast press release June 2025, Mintlify/GitBook own docs). Independent third-party counts confirm the spec's self-reported 'thousands of sites' (Originality.ai ~36,120 instances by May 2026, 8.8x YoY; Rankability 8.7% of top-1000). But the two consumption-side claims were 2-1 splits: the spec itself only describes intended behavior, and reality is contested — coding agents (Cursor/Claude Code/Copilot) reportedly fetch it in dev-tool contexts (~51.8% reachability) while Ahrefs found 97% of files across 137k domains got ZERO AI requests, and Google/Mueller stated Google does not consume it. The publishing/consumption gap is precisely the open risk for code-repo worthwhileness.
